title: Failure-Resilient Multi-Robot Coordination with 𝑘-Connectivity Constrained Submodular Maximization

paper.title: Failure-Resilient Multi-Robot Coordination with k k -Connectivity Constrained Submodular Maximization
paper.abstract: Abstract Multi-robot coordination is essential in applications such as coverage, target tracking, and information gathering, where robots must jointly select actions to maximize team performance. Submodular maximization provides an effective framework for such coordination, and resilient variants further account for robot failures or adversarial removals. However, existing methods typically overlook the impact of robot loss on the communication network, which may disconnect the surviving team and prevent continued coordination. To address this issue, we introduce Resilient k k -Connected Submodular Maximization, which jointly considers task performance, resilience, and communication connectivity. The resulting feasible family is not a matroid, preventing a direct application of classical curvature-greedy guarantees. We overcome this challenge through a Menger-based connectivity reduction, a connectivity-aware greedy algorithm with a feasibility-preserving fallback, and a new curvature-based analysis that captures the cost of enforcing connectivity through a single factor ρ \rho . Our method achieves a worst-case post-failure objective within a factor [ max ⁡ ( 1 − ν f ​ ( ℐ ) , h ⁡ ( N , β ) ) ] 2 ​ ρ ​ 1 κ f ​ ( 1 − e − κ f ) [\max(1-\nu_{f}(\mathcal{I}),h(N,\beta))]^{2}\rho\frac{1}{\kappa_{f}}(1-e^{-\kappa_{f}}) of the optimal connectivity-respecting resilient assignment, while recovering the classical unconstrained guarantee in the appropriate limits. Experiments on multi-robot target tracking validate the proposed method and characterize the practical impact of connectivity constraints.

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: Multi-robot systems provide scalable solutions to applications such as environmental monitoring, target tracking, search and rescue, and collaborative exploration [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] . In many of these settings, the robots must coordinate their sensing or motion decisions to maximize a common team objective [ 5 ] . Submodular set functions provide a natural mathematical framework for such coordination by capturing the principle of diminishing returns: the marginal benefit of adding an additional robot decreases as more robots are already selected. Many commonly used objectives, including mutual information [ 6 ] , area coverage [ 7 ] , number of observed targets [ 8 ] , and sensor-measurement entropy [ 9 ] are monotone submodular [ 10 ] . This structure enables computationally efficient greedy algorithms with well-established constant-factor performance guarantees, as reviewed in Section II . Fig. 1 : The core structural conflict in multi-robot deployments. (Left) Aerial teams face adversarial attacks or failures removing up to β \beta nodes. (Middle) Existing frameworks treat requirements in isolation, in which standard resilient maximization risks post-attack fragmentation, while standard connectivity assumes a failure-free environment. (Right) Our framework resolves this by achieving simultaneous adversarial resilience and ( β + 1 ) (\beta+1) -vertex-connectivity, ensuring the surviving team remains structurally connected and performant. Classical submodular maximization, however, typically assumes that the selected robots remain available throughout execution. In practice, robots may be lost due to hardware failures, communication interference, denial-of-service attacks, or other adverse events. This has motivated resilient submodular maximization, where the team is selected so that the objective remains large even after a bounded number of robots are removed [ 8 , 11 , 12 ] . Existing resilient formulations primarily focus on preserving submodular objective performance after such removals. Yet, critically, robot loss can disrupt the communication network among surviving robots. A team might therefore retain high sensing or coverage capacity after failures while becoming disconnected and rendered unable to continue coordinated operation. Communication connectivity and resilience have both been studied extensively, but largely as separate requirements. In this work, we consider them jointly and ask how to select robot actions so that the team achieves a high submodular objective while remaining connected even after adversarial robot removals. We refer to this problem as Resilient k k -Connected Submodular Maximization (see Fig. 1 ). The joint treatment is substantially more challenging than simply combining two existing constraints. Resilience requires accounting for the worst-case subset of removed robots, while connectivity is a global property whose feasibility depends on which robots survive. This interaction also breaks key structures used in existing approximation analysis. In the resilient maximization framework of Tzoumas et al. [ 11 ] , robustness is achieved by constructing a sacrificial “bait” set of β \beta high-value robots together with a greedily selected remainder. Under a connectivity requirement, however, the adversary determines which robots are removed, and the worst-case removal need not coincide with the bait set. Consequently, enforcing connectivity only on the non-bait robots does not guarantee that the surviving team remains connected. Moreover, the constraint of selecting one trajectory per robot together with a global vertex-connectivity requirement does not form a matroid. As a result, classical curvature-based greedy guarantees cannot be applied directly and must be re-established for the connectivity-constrained resilient setting. We make the following contributions: • We formulate resilient submodular maximization under a ( β + 1 ) (\beta{+}1) -vertex-connectivity constraint and show that the family of partial, connectivity-feasible selections is not a matroid (Proposition 1 ), identifying precisely why the classical greedy analysis fails to transfer. • We introduce a connectivity filter with a rigid-shift fallback across both bait and greedy stages, show it guarantees a feasible, ( β + 1 ) (\beta{+}1) -connected output that survives any removal of size at most β \beta regardless of composition (Proposition 2 ), and re-derive the curvature-greedy bound against a connectivity-respecting benchmark (Lemma 1 ), isolating the filter’s entire cost into a single interpretable constant ρ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \rho\in[0,1] . • We prove a resilient, connectivity-preserving approximation guarantee (Theorem 1 ) and empirically corroborate the algorithm’s feasibility, the price of connectivity, and the squared resilience factor (Section V ).

sections.heading: IV Methodology and Theoretical Analysis
sections.text: Our algorithm mirrors the bait-plus-greedy structure of Tzoumas et al. [ 11 ] and Zhou et al. [ 8 ] , augmented with a connectivity filter and a rigid-shift fallback in both stages. The analysis is in two parts. First, connectivity and survivability (Section IV-B ) follow essentially by construction and are dealt with in Proposition 2 . Second, the substance of the analysis is the performance bound (Sections IV-D – IV-E ), which quantifies the effect of the connectivity constraint on the usual resilient greedy choices, and how this constraint impacts the approximation guarantee.

sections.text: Our experiment objectives are (i) to characterize the connectivity penalty ρ \rho across communication densities and team sizes, establishing that it remains bounded away from zero in realistic instances, (ii) to validate the feasibility of Algorithm 1 ’s outputs (Proposition 2 ), (iii) to test the squared resilience factor derived in ( 9 ), and (iv) to evaluate the algorithm’s operational resilience and connectivity maintenance over multi-planning cycle deployments.

sections.text: Our central claim is that RES-CON preserves connectivity under repeated adversarial attack where connectivity-blind methods fragment. We test this over a T T -planning cycle horizon with moving targets, sweeping r c r_{c} relative to the percolation threshold and measuring both the worst-case-survivor disconnection rate and cumulative target tracking. sections.heading: VI Conclusion and Future Work
sections.text: We introduced resilient submodular maximization under a ( β + 1 ) (\beta{+}1) -vertex-connectivity constraint, jointly capturing adversarial robustness and communication network integrity for multi-robot teams. Several directions remain open. First, the squared resilience factor is established under the intra-stage hypothesis of Proposition 3 and corroborated empirically. A proof that this hypothesis holds unconditionally for disk-graph geometries under bounded motion would bolster the idea. Second, deriving a geometric lower bound for ρ \rho would convert the penalty into a computable quantity, making ( 9 ) a fully unconditional guarantee on non-degenerate instances. Finally, a hardware demonstration on an aerial or ground fleet would validate the connectivity guarantee under real communication models.

I Introduction Multi-robot systems provide scalable solutions to applications such as environmental monitoring, target tracking, search and rescue, and collaborative exploration [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] . In many of these settings, the robots must coordinate their sensing or motion decisions to maximize a common team objective [ 5 ] . Submodular set functions provide a natural mathematical framework for such coordination by capturing the principle of diminishing returns: the marginal benefit of adding an additional robot decreases as more robots are already selected. Many commonly used objectives, including mutual information [ 6 ] , area coverage [ 7 ] , number of observed targets [ 8 ] , and sensor-measurement entropy [ 9 ] are monotone submodular [ 10 ] . This structure enables computationally efficient greedy algorithms with well-established constant-factor performance guarantees, as reviewed in Section II . Fig. 1 : The core structural conflict in multi-robot deployments. (Left) Aerial teams face adversarial attacks or failures removing up to β  eta nodes. (Middle) Existing frameworks treat requirements in isolation, in which standard resilient maximization risks post-attack fragmentation, while standard connectivity assumes a failure-free environment. (Right) Our framework resolves this by achieving simultaneous adversarial resilience and ( β + 1 ) ( eta+1) -vertex-connectivity, ensuring the surviving team remains structurally connected and performant. Classical submodular maximization, however, typically assumes that the selected robots remain available throughout execution. In practice, robots may be lost due to hardware failures, communication interference, denial-of-service attacks, or other adverse events. This has motivated resilient submodular maximization, where the team is selected so that the objective remains large even after a bounded number of robots are removed [ 8 , 11 , 12 ] . Existing resilient formulations primarily focus on preserving submodular objective performance after such removals. Yet, critically, robot loss can disrupt the communication network among surviving robots. A team might therefore retain high sensing or coverage capacity after failures while becoming disconnected and rendered unable to continue coordinated operation. Communication connectivity and resilience have both been studied extensively, but largely as separate requirements. In this work, we consider them jointly and ask how to select robot actions so that the team achieves a high submodular objective while remaining connected even after adversarial robot removals. We refer to this problem as Resilient k k -Connected Submodular Maximization (see Fig. 1 ). The joint treatment is substantially more challenging than simply combining two existing constraints. Resilience requires accounting for the worst-case subset of removed robots, while connectivity is a global property whose feasibility depends on which robots survive. This interaction also breaks key structures used in existing approximation analysis. In the resilient maximization framework of Tzoumas et al. [ 11 ] , robustness is achieved by constructing a sacrificial “bait” set of β  eta high-value robots together with a greedily selected remainder. Under a connectivity requirement, however, the adversary determines which robots are removed, and the worst-case removal need not coincide with the bait set. Consequently, enforcing connectivity only on the non-bait robots does not guarantee that the surviving team remains connected. Moreover, the constraint of selecting one trajectory per robot together with a global vertex-connectivity requirement does not form a matroid. As a result, classical curvature-based greedy guarantees cannot be applied directly and must be re-established for the connectivity-constrained resilient setting. We make the following contributions: • We formulate resilient submodular maximization under a ( β + 1 ) ( eta{+}1) -vertex-connectivity constraint and show that the family of partial, connectivity-feasible selections is not a matroid (Proposition 1 ), identifying precisely why the classical greedy analysis fails to transfer. • We introduce a connectivity filter with a rigid-shift fallback across both bait and greedy stages, show it guarantees a feasible, ( β + 1 ) ( eta{+}1) -connected output that survives any removal of size at most β  eta regardless of composition (Proposition 2 ), and re-derive the curvature-greedy bound against a connectivity-respecting benchmark (Lemma 1 ), isolating the filter’s entire cost into a single interpretable constant ρ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] ho\in[0,1] . • We prove a resilient, connectivity-preserving approximation guarantee (Theorem 1 ) and empirically corroborate the algorithm’s feasibility, the price of connectivity, and the squared resilience factor (Section V ).
